item.title: Firefighters contain fire at ABC Junkyard in Waiawa after explosions reported
item.dc:creator: Ben Gutierrez, HNN Staff
item.description: Firefighters reported a large pile of miscellaneous recyclable material was burning.
item.content:encoded:
WAIAWA (HawaiiNewsNow) - Honolulu firefighters have contained a fire that broke out Wednesday afternoon at ABC Junkyard in Waiawa, an auto salvage yard with a history of code violations and prior fires.

According to the Honolulu Fire Department, firefighters responded shortly before 3 p.m. to the property along the 800 block of Lehua Avenue.

Nearby residents reported hearing explosions coming from the facility as crews arrived on scene.

“There was a lot of explosions, big ones, you know,” said Andre Perez. “I can imagine acetylene tanks, something like that. Big, loud explosions.”

“There was probably at least eight, and then I left, I wasn’t going to stick around,” said Corrie Young. “I was scared, yeah. Really big explosions.”

Firefighters reported a large pile of miscellaneous recyclable material was burning. Wind from the south sent columns of thick black smoke over the H-1 Freeway and into Pearl City.

“Most of that trash looks synthetic. So this fire — the smoke was probably really toxic and it’s something that we’ve been expressing concern about for a long time, for over a year,” said Perez.

HFD said a total of 11 fire companies, including crews from Honolulu and federal fire agencies, responded to the fire.

“We’re lucky that it happened on rainy day,” said Camille Kalama, another neighboring resident. “Hopefully that helped dampen the fire. But this shouldn’t be happening in a neighborhood with residents all around us.”

The fire was contained just before 5 p.m. Crews will continue to perform overhaul tactics to search for hidden fires to prevent rekindling.

Smoke advisory

The Hawaii Department of Health has lifted a smoke advisory that went into effect Wednesday for parts of Pearl City due to the fire at ABC Towing.

DOH on-site coordinators were dispatched to the scene and had advised residents and visitors in the surrounding area, especially those with pre-existing respiratory conditions such as asthma, bronchitis and emphysema, to take precautionary measures or leave the area until the fire was contained and the smoke subsided.

DOH advises individuals impacted by smoke from the fire at ABC Towing & Parts to:

  • Avoid outdoor activities to reduce exposure and minimize health risks. This tip is especially important for children, seniors and individuals with conditions such as chronic lung and heart disease.
  • Stay indoors and close all windows and doors. If using an air conditioner, set it to recirculate the air.
  • If you must leave the affected area, turn on your vehicle’s air conditioner and set it to the recirculate option.
  • Always keep medications on hand.
  • Prescribed medications for respiratory illnesses should be taken on schedule.
  • If you experience any health problems, contact your doctor as soon as possible.
  • Do not smoke and avoid second-hand smoke.
  • Drink lots of fluids to avoid dehydration.
  • Have family emergency plans prepared and ready.

No injuries have been reported.

Neighbors were also concerned that the dump is still operating, since they mentioned there was a cease-and-desist order.

“It’s permitted to be a junkyard for cars, automotive junkyard. But it’s been turned into a landfill where they’re receiving truckloads of roll-off dumpsters every day with mixed trash, construction trash,” said Perez.

“We’re getting bombarded by the smoke, by dust on a daily basis, by the noise, and just by the threat of having this illegal landfill right next door,” said Kalama.

The junkyard owner has said that he is still allowed to operate while he appeals the orders.

item.title: Senator introduces bill to protect workers during AI boom
item.dc:creator: Caitrin Assaf
item.description: With artificial intelligence becoming a hot topic on Capitol Hill, one lawmaker is working to make sure Congress gets ahead of the issue - protecting Americans and guaranteeing AI works for them.
item.content:encoded:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Artificial intelligence has become a recent hot topic of debate on Capitol Hill, as lawmakers consider how to move forward with the quickly changing technology. Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly (D) is one lawmaker proposing legislation that supports humans while also considering the relevance of the tech.

“This is something we have to tackle immediately,” Kelly said.

What to do about the rise and evolution of artificial intelligence has become a sticking point on Capitol Hill. With the technology both a benefit and a possible risk, Kelly says it’s important to get ahead of the trend.

“You know when I used to fly the space shuttle, the master alarms flashing on the instrument panel, you gotta take action. You look at the data, you come up with a plan, you execute the plan. That’s this moment with this technology,” Kelly said.

Kelly said AI has integrated itself into Americans’ everyday lives while also posing a risk to workers, who could soon see their positions filled by technological advancements.

Kelly introduced the Make AI Work for Americans Act, legislation that would guarantee companies benefiting most from AI invest in workers and pay their fair share, mitigating damage from technology poised to replace the human workforce.

“There are estimates out there that possibly millions of Americans lose their jobs because of this technology. We have to have an answer for that,” Kelly said.

The legislation is one proposal amid increased debate on artificial intelligence. The debate comes the same week President Donald Trump hosted top tech leaders at the White House to praise the development of what he calls “super intelligence.”

Kelly said any evolution must come with strict guardrails and should not rely on companies to self-police. He said that begins with an understanding of the basic workings of AI.

“So we can introduce good legislation that will work,” Kelly said.

item.title: More than a dozen sickened in parasite outbreak linked to hotel pool, health officials say
item.dc:creator: KPTV News staff, Jordan Gartner
item.description: Public health officials say more than a dozen people were sickened by a parasite linked to a hotel swimming pool.
item.content:encoded:
BOTHELL, Wash. (KPTV/Gray News) — Public health officials say more than a dozen people were sickened by a parasite linked to a hotel swimming pool.

Health officials in King County shared that an investigation was opened earlier this summer after 14 people reported falling ill after swimming in the pool at McMenamins Anderson School, an entertainment destination and boutique hotel built inside a converted junior high school, in late August.

The investigation found that an outbreak of cryptosporidiosis was linked to the hotel pool, with laboratory tests confirming the illness was caused by cryptosporidium, a microscopic parasite.

Those who were sickened were said to have symptoms such as diarrhea, stomach cramps, nausea and fever that started days after visiting the pool area.

Investigators suspect the parasite spread when an infected swimmer entered the pool.

Officials noted that the facility was well-maintained, followed all county health and safety regulations, and had no violations during a September inspection.

But because the microscopic parasite is highly chlorine-resistant, it can survive in properly treated pools for several days.

No hospitalizations or deaths were reported in this case, with Washington health officials saying the outbreak now appears to be over.

Cryptosporidium was also the parasite that caused an outbreak of explosive diarrhea across the U.S. also earlier this year.

Health officials emphasized that swimmers should avoid public pools for at least two weeks after recovering from diarrhea or vomiting and should shower with soap before swimming.

item.title: Supreme Court to review immigrant detention policy
item.dc:creator: Brendan Cullerton
item.description: The Supreme Court announced Thursday it will review the Trump administration’s policy of detaining immigrants who entered the country illegally without a bond hearing.
item.content:encoded:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The Supreme Court announced Thursday it will review the Trump administration’s policy of detaining immigrants who entered the country illegally without a bond hearing.

Previously, most immigrants who entered the country illegally were given a bond hearing, provided they did not have a criminal record, and were detained away from the border. The Trump administration has ended that practice, and the new policy is now before the Supreme Court.

The case revolves around a Brazilian citizen the Trump administration argues entered the country illegally two decades ago and applied for asylum in 2016. The man has never been charged with a crime besides illegal entry, but was placed in detention following a 2025 traffic stop and kept there.

In July, the Trump administration began the policy of mandatory detention without bond. The policy shift comes from a new interpretation of a 1990s immigration law.

Most lower courts have ruled that detaining immigrants indefinitely without a bond hearing is illegal, but the Fifth and Eighth circuit courts have upheld the new policy.

The high court is expected to hear the case in the next few months, with a decision expected by the end of June 2027.

item.title: Walmart recalls nearly 4.5 million grill wire brushes. Here are the impacted brushes
item.dc:creator: Debra Worley
item.description: Walmart is recalling nearly 4.5 million Expert Grill wire brushes due to loose bristles posing an ingestion hazard. Check the recalled model numbers and refund info.
item.content:encoded:
(Gray News) - Walmart is recalling nearly 4.5 million grill brushes because small metal wire bristles can detach, stick to grills or food, and cause severe internal injuries requiring surgery if swallowed.

The recall covers approximately 4,477,655 Expert Grill metal wire bristle brushes sold individually and as part of grilling tool sets, according to the Consumer Product Safety Commission.

The brushes feature black plastic or stainless steel handles, and several models include an attached metal scraper.

Products were sold at Walmart stores nationwide and online at Walmart.com from January 2021 through August 2026 for between $1 and $28.

No injuries or incidents have been reported, according to the CPSC notice.

Recalled models

The recall includes five specific models. Consumers can locate the model number on the product packaging or on a sticker or tag attached directly to the brush:

  • EX5607031616002: Expert Grill 16-inch Steel Fiber Scrub Brush and Scraper for Grills (sold January 2025 to August 2026)
  • EX5607031616003: Expert Grill Handheld Steel Fiber Scrub Brush with Ergonomic Handle for Grill Cleaning (sold January 2025 to August 2026)
  • XG1310700206: Expert Grill 21-inch 3-Head Grill Brush with Stainless Steel Bristles and Soft-Grip Handle (sold January 2022 to August 2026)
  • XG1136178597003: Expert Grill Long Handle Grill Brush with Scraper, 17.7-inch (sold January 2021 to August 2026)
  • XG1410700124: Expert Grill Grilling Accessories BBQ Grill Tools Set, 10-Piece Stainless Steel Grill Kit (sold December 2023 to August 2026)

Refund and contact information

Consumers should immediately stop using the recalled brushes and contact Walmart to receive a full refund or store credit valid in stores or online. Customers will be instructed to either return the product to a store or discard it.

Walmart can be reached toll-free at 800-925-6278 from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. CT Monday through Friday, or online through the company’s product recalls page.

item.title: Millions in Amazon settlement payouts are rolling out. Are you eligible?
item.dc:creator: Jordan Gartner
item.description: Automatic payments as part of an expanded federal settlement over billing and cancellation practices involving Amazon have started going out.
item.content:encoded:
(Gray News) - Automatic payments as part of an expanded federal settlement over billing and cancellation practices involving Amazon have reportedly started going out.

Last month, the Federal Trade Commission announced that Amazon was accelerating and widening consumer refund payouts stemming from a $2.5 billion deceptive enrollment settlement.

Under the historic September 2025 settlement of the FTC’s allegations, Amazon was required to pay up to $1.5 billion in redress to consumers harmed by the company’s deceptive Prime enrollment practices in addition to a $1 billion civil penalty.

According to the FTC, those automatic payments started rolling out Thursday via PayPal, Venmo or mailed check.

The eligibility requirement also expanded beyond low-use subscribers to include millions who used between 11 and 20 Prime benefits over a one-year period.

“The revised order will ensure more consumers who were harmed by Amazon’s deceptive enrollment and cancellation practices benefit from the FTC’s historic settlement,” Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said.

Additionally, the individual payment cap could be as high as $200.

Those who have already cashed earlier checks could see an additional automatic supplemental payment of up to $149 starting in April 2027.

The settlement noted that customers do not have to file any claims or forms.

But the FTC warned that anyone reaching out claiming to be from the agency or asking for money or personal banking details to claim a refund is running a potential scam.

item.title: Witnesses describe Christa Pike ‘snoring’ and ‘looking around’ during botched execution attempt
item.dc:creator: Li Cohen, Akim Powell
item.description: Christa Pike remains alive after Tennessee officials attempted to execute her by lethal injection, with witnesses describing disturbing moments during the failed attempt.
item.content:encoded:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - Christa Pike remains alive after officials attempted to execute her by lethal injection, with witnesses describing “haunting” moments during the failed attempt.

The state tried to execute her by lethal injection on Wednesday, but neither the initial nor backup dose of pentobarbital killed her.

“Christa is alive right now. We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment,” Spivey said during a news conference.

Witnesses say she was snoring when the execution chamber’s microphone was cut off more than an hour into the attempt.

Attorneys say at least seven needles were used in her left arm alone. They described her physical reactions, including ragged breathing, looking around and complaining of a burning sensation.

The failed execution amounted to “torture,” her lawyers said, and they called for her death sentence to be commuted.

“I’m haunted by last night,” he said. “What I saw last night is not something that should ever, ever happen again.”

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death for killing Colleen Slemmer in 1995.

Slemmer was 19 years old when she was killed after being lured to an isolated area on the University of Tennessee agricultural campus. Both Slemmer and Pike were enrolled in Job Corps at the time.

Pike and two co-defendants, Tadaryl Shipp and Shadolla Peterson, were convicted in 1996. Testimony showed the trio tortured Slemmer, carved a pentagram into her chest and Pike kept a piece of Slemmer’s skull as a souvenir.

Pike is currently receiving “life-saving medical care.”

item.title: Rapper Rick Ross denied special treatment in court as judge tells him ‘I don’t know who you are’
item.dc:creator: Emily Van de Riet
item.description: Rapper Rick Ross, born William Leonard Roberts, is facing charges for an alleged domestic violence issue in August.
item.content:encoded:
MIAMI BEACH, Fla. (Gray News) — Rapper Rick Ross, born William Leonard Roberts, is facing charges for an alleged domestic violence issue in August.

But the judge Ross appeared in front of Thursday did not know who he was.

Brad Horenstein, Ross’ lawyer, wanted his client’s release expedited.

“Mr. Roberts is a celebrity, and so I don’t know...” Horenstein said.

“What does that mean?” the judge responded.

“I don’t know to whatever degree your honor can, but I’d ask that that his release be expedited. He’s in a red jumpsuit and for purposes of his safety. I don’t know what your honor can do, but, I don’t know,” Horenstein said.

The judge then said hello to Ross and said he would not get special treatment.

“Hi, Mr. Roberts. I have no idea who you are, except as somebody here in the court who’s going to be treated fairly just like everybody else here,” she said.

Ross faces a felony charge of battery by strangulation, as well as a misdemeanor battery charge, according to online court records.

An attorney for Ross, 50, said in a statement that Ross is being wrongfully accused by an ex-girlfriend whose motivations are unclear.

“The ex did not even file a police report until a month after the claimed incident allegedly took place,” defense attorney Steve Sadow said in the statement. “Mr. Roberts is innocent and has pled not guilty to the charges. He respectfully requests that his friends, fans and the general public not prejudge the situation and allow the judicial process to run its course.”

Jail records showed that Ross was being held Thursday morning on $5,000 bail. He was later released. An arraignment is scheduled for Oct. 22.

media:content.media:description: The judge Rick Ross appeared in front of Thursday did not know who he was.

item.title: Patriots tight end Eli Raridon and wife announce death of newborn son
item.dc:creator: Dorothy Sedovic
item.description: New England Patriots tight end Eli Raridon and his wife, Anna Raridon, announced the death of their newborn son.
item.content:encoded:
(Gray News) - New England Patriots tight end Eli Raridon and his wife, Anna Raridon, announced the death of their newborn son.

“Our angel, Peter James Raridon, was born on September 11,” the couple announced on Instagram.

In the announcement, the couple said that they learned during the 20-week anatomy scan that their son had anencephaly, which they described as “a fatal condition in which he would not survive outside the womb.”

“While we are absolutely devastated that we were unable to bring our baby boy home, I am grateful to have loved him deeply, kept him safe, and had been his home for the past 9 months before he was called back to Heaven,” the post read.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, anencephaly is a birth defect in which the baby forms without parts of the brain and skull. The CDC said that almost all babies with anencephaly die shortly after birth and there is currently no cure or treatment.

“I believe our little boy was lovingly knitted together in the womb by God, knowing how deeply he would be loved by our families, our friends, Eli, and me. Though his time with us was brief, his life still precious, his purpose still meaningful, and he will forever be a part of our story,” the post said.

Eli and Anna Raridon were married on May 25, 2025. They announced in an Instagram post on March 31 that they were expecting their first child.

“I have loved you every second of your life & will miss you every second of mine. What a sweet sweet reunion ours will be,” the couple’s post said.

This is Eli Raridon’s first season with the New England Patriots. He was picked by the team during the third round of the 2026 draft. Prior to that, he played for Notre Dame.

item.title: SNAP benefit changes are in effect for millions of recipients. Here’s what you need to know
item.dc:creator: Jordan Gartner
item.description: Millions of Americans who depend on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program will see changes, including a slight increase in the cost of living.
item.content:encoded:
WASHINGTON (Gray News) - Millions of Americans who depend on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program will be seeing changes Thursday, including a slight cost-of-living increase.

Every year on Oct. 1, the federal government adjusts its monthly SNAP benefits to account for inflation.

For the upcoming fiscal year, the maximum SNAP benefit for a one-person household will rise by about $8 per month, while the maximum benefit for a household of four will increase by about $29 per month.

Those numbers translate to a maximum monthly benefit of $306 for a single-person household and $1,023 for a household of four.

Federal officials note that benefits vary based on different household circumstances, and residents in Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands will see higher maximums.

The inflation adjustments are intended to help families with the rising cost of food.

Food prices in the United States have increased by about 2.7% between August 2025 and August 2026, according to the United States Department of Agriculture.

The USDA reported earlier this year that more than 37 million people received SNAP benefits, with the program also seeing a drop of nearly 5 million recipients from a year earlier.

More information for those interested in applying for SNAP benefits can also be found online.

item.title: Girl, 11, will learn her fate in trial over brutal rape and assault of a 5-year-old
item.dc:creator: 19 News Digital Team, Gray News staff
item.description: The trial for the 11-year-old girl accused in the brutal rape and assault of a five-year-old girl wrapped up in Cuyahoga County Juvenile Court.
item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND (WOIO/Gray News) - The trial for the 11-year-old girl accused in the brutal rape and assault of a 5-year-old girl wrapped up in Cuyahoga County Juvenile Court Wednesday afternoon.

Judge Kristin Sweeney will release her decision on Friday.

What happened

Prosecutors said the 11-year-old, addressed as M.H. in court, and a now 10-year-old boy attacked the girl in a field in Cleveland on Sept. 13, 2025.

The victim’s clothes were removed, according to testimony, and she was strangled with her own shirt.

The 10-year-old boy, addressed as M.B. during the trial, pleaded guilty Monday to attempted rape and felonious assault.

He testified against the 11-year-old girl Wednesday and described what he claims M.H. said while strangling the victim with a shirt.

“This is what bad girls get for following people,” said M.B.

He says M.H. also ordered him to tell anyone about what happened.

“How were you feeling when she told you that?” asked the prosecution. “Scared,” said M.B.

He is scheduled to be back in court on Nov. 20 and could face probation or placement in a residential treatment facility.

Victim’s mom takes the stand

On Tuesday, the mom of the victim took the stand and testified that her daughter spent several weeks in the hospital following the attack.

She also described the emotional toll the attack has had on her little girl.

“When we left the hospital, she went through severe behavioral changes. She kept saying she’s not pretty anymore. She kept saying earth is a bad place,” said the mom.

Previous coverage:

  • Children charged in brutal attack on 5-year-old Cleveland girl to undergo competency restoration
  • Cleveland police connect kid suspects to beating; mother describes 5-year-old as ‘unrecognizable’
  • Prosecutors charge 2 children, 9 and 10, in brutal attack on 5-year-old Cleveland girl

Case background

The Cleveland Division of Police Sex Crimes and Child Abuse Unit investigated the case.

In October 2025, prosecutors charged the 11-year-old girl and then nine-year-old boy with attempted murder, rape, felonious assault, kidnapping and strangulation.

On April 1, Judge Sweeney ordered the two children to undergo competency restoration before they could stand trial.

According to court records, a change in the 11-year-old’s placement was necessary to get a true assessment of her competency.

When a placement was not found, prosecutors requested she be held in the detention center during the restoration process.

The court said returning to her home was not in her best interest, and the Court Diagnostics Clinic provided competency restoration services at the detention center.

Both children were previously held on home detention.

After a period of court-ordered rehabilitation, the children were later found competent to stand trial.

item.title: Court documents detail hours leading up to 2 Ole Miss students’ suspected overdose deaths
item.dc:creator: Joyce Peterson, Lydian Coombs (Kennin)
item.description: Court documents reveal what investigators found after two Ole Miss students died, including SMAX Pseudo-DHM and other kratom-like products.
item.content:encoded:
OXFORD, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) — Mississippi leaders and lawmakers are calling for a crackdown on kratom and kratom-like products after two Ole Miss students died last week.

Toxicology tests are incomplete, and the autopsies on both young men are still pending.

But court documents filed Monday reveal what 18-year-old Aidan Hamilton and 20-year-old Robert Strang were doing in the hours and days before their suspected overdose deaths.

Investigators with Lafayette County Metro Narcotics previously said store-bought kratom was found in both students’ rooms.

On Sept. 30, Metro Narcotics clarified the information in an earlier statement to WMC:

“During the investigations, packaging associated with kratom-related products was discovered at both locations. This information prompted law enforcement to issue a public safety warning out of an abundance of caution.

That warning was not a declaration that kratom or any specific substance caused either death. It was a proactive effort to inform the public of a potential danger while investigators worked to determine the facts.”

Authorities were able to determine where the young men bought the drugs. The investigation now stretches from Lafayette County into neighboring Yalobusha County at a convenience store about 20 miles from the Ole Miss campus.

What investigators found in Hamilton’s dorm room

Hamilton died in his on-campus dorm room on Sept. 21.

Court documents show the coroner and medical personnel on the scene said the young man “could have died due to a pulmonary edema, consistent with a drug overdose.”

Hamilton’s roommate told investigators that Hamilton “smoked a lot of marijuana from pens and pipes,” “would keep his marijuana in a safe,” and “used it a lot, so much so, he had a terrible cough.”

But investigators are focusing on SMAX Pseudo-DHM pills, a chemically manipulated product, found on Hamilton’s dresser in his room at Stewart Hall.

Statements filed by Caleb East, an agent with the Lafayette County Metro Narcotics Unit, noted that “agents are aware that these are often sold as a kratom-like substance at gas stations or tobacco shops.”

Mississippi Department of Public Safety Commissioner Sean Tindell said, “We’re wanting to test those and make sure that anything that’s in there… it’s not being laced with any other chemicals, or there’s no other harmful chemicals in that product.”

What investigators found at Strang’s home

At the scene of Strang’s death, inside his off-campus home on Van Buren Avenue, investigators said they found 20 to 30 nitrous oxide cans.

His roommates said Strang “would use whippets daily,” the street term given to the popular party drug. Strang’s housemates also said he would use “sometimes two to three cans a week.”

Investigators also found a packet of SMAX on his nightstand in packaging similar to what was found in Hamilton’s dorm.

Roommates said Strang took a Xanax bar around 4 p.m. Sunday. He was last seen in the kitchen around midnight. His body was discovered the next day in his bedroom at 3:30 p.m.

Doctors warn about kratom and synthetic kratom-like products

Following the student deaths, Mississippi doctors are again warning about the dangers of products marketed as kratom, a natural leaf that can be tainted with other chemicals or offered in versions that are made synthetically with illegal substances, referred to as “gas station heroin.”

Dr. Lucas Trautman, medical director at the Oxford Treatment Center, told WMC, “It’s being sold in gas stations as sort of ‘natural’... that’s the buzz you hear with it... in order to help you with pain or sleep. Well, it’s just an opioid, so people get addicted to it, too, and have severe withdrawals.”

Family physician Dr. Jennifer Bryan said, “I would urge the public that if you see ‘natural,’ natural does not mean safe. It’s not synonymous. We still don’t know what’s inside that package. No matter what the label says, you don’t know what’s inside that package. The regulation is very loose.”

SMAX Pseudo-DHM is a synthetic drug marketed as a kratom-like substance. But investigators say it has a “significantly higher potency compared to natural leaf products.”

In the affidavit filed in the Third District Circuit Court of Mississippi on Sept. 28, following undercover operations at two retail stores, drug agents said the ingredients can be “produced fully synthetically in clandestine laboratories.”

The affidavit lists the ingredients of SMAX Pseudo-DHM as pseudoindoxyl, MGM-15 and 7-hydroxymitragynine.

The DEA temporarily placed mitragynine, pseudoindoxyl and MGM-15 on the Schedule I list on Aug. 26, 2026.

Schedule I drugs, including heroin, LSD and ecstasy, are illegal in the U.S. under federal law.

“Synthetic mitragynine compounds can be significantly stronger than morphine,” East wrote in the affidavit, “and carry a high risk of severe addiction, overdose and death.”

Where the drugs were purchased

Investigators with Metro Narcotics say Strang bought his SMAX product at Express Mart #7 in Water Valley in Yalobusha County. Bank records show he visited the store twice — once on Sept. 9 and again on Sept. 11.

The store is about a 20- to 30-minute drive from the Ole Miss campus.

Undercover officers bought more of the product a day after his death.

Court documents say the clerk said the store was out of the 200-mg version but sold “another form of the SMAX Pseudo-DHM pills consistent with the packages found at the Strang scene.”

The pills were sent to a forensic lab in Columbus, Mississippi, for analysis.

Agents returned to Express Mart #7 on Sept. 23 and bought more of the pills, this time sending them to a crime lab in Florida for analysis.

Investigators say records show Aidan Hamilton made multiple purchases at Puffs Vape Tobacco and Beer in Oxford. Bank records provided by his parents showed he visited the store and made purchases on Sept. 9, Sept. 14 and Sept. 20, one day before his death.

On Sept. 24, Metro Narcotics agents sent a confidential informant into the store, equipped with audio and video equipment. The informant tried to buy nitrous oxide, but the clerk told him that the store didn’t have any.

The affidavit says the clerk then offered to sell the informant marijuana from a jar and pre-rolled joints. The informant declined, but later asked if the store sold “7 O Kratom based pills.” The clerk said yes.

Records show an employee told an undercover informant to “be careful taking the pills because people are dying from them.”

Two employees of that store were arrested, and 500 units of kratom and kratom-like products were seized. The Metro Narcotics team also found an assortment of “THC cartridges, gummies, pre-rolls and other suspected THC substances.”

Recreational marijuana is still classified as an illegal Schedule I drug in the U.S.

Possible legislative action

The scope and impact of the Ole Miss deaths investigation could lead to legislative change.

Commissioner Tindell said, “Once kratom is banned locally, it’s still only a misdemeanor. And so I think one of the things the legislature is going to look at and consider next year… is, are we at the point where we need a statewide ban on kratom?”

Kratom is currently banned in the City of Oxford and Lafayette County. And again, the ingredients in the SMAX products found in the students’ rooms — products sold by two retail establishments — are illegal under federal law.

The students’ toxicology reports are being expedited and could come back as soon as this week. Until that happens, their causes of death are pending.

The American Kratom Association held a news conference in Oxford on Wednesday to defend natural kratom and differentiate it from the manufactured products that authorities said were found in the students’ rooms.

item.title: Personal bankruptcy filings up nearly 50% since 2022, analysis finds
item.dc:creator: Rachel DePompa
item.description: Personal bankruptcy filings are up nearly 50% since 2022, a new LendingTree analysis finds. Here is what's driving the surge and how to get help.
item.content:encoded:
(InvestigateTV) — Personal bankruptcy filings have jumped nearly 50% since 2022, according to a new LendingTree analysis, as inflation on housing, insurance, groceries and health care, combined with high interest rates, pushes families deeper into credit card debt.

About 1,400 people a day are now turning to the courts for relief. The biggest spikes are in the South, and most filings are the more severe Chapter 7 bankruptcies, which wipe out many debts but also significantly damage credit.

Matt Schulz, with LendingTree, said reaching the point of filing for bankruptcy typically follows a long period of financial strain.

“Anytime you’re talking about bankruptcy, it’s a really big deal, because bankruptcy is generally the end of a long, difficult period that somebody has faced over the course of months or years, and they’ve decided that they really have no other choice,” Schulz said.

Schulz said filing for bankruptcy can create financial challenges that last seven to 10 years. He recommends addressing missed or late payments as early as possible.

“It’s a whole lot easier to go to a creditor when you are saying, ‘Hey, I think I may be late with a payment this month or in the coming months,’ than to go to them and say, ‘Hey, I haven’t paid you in three months, can you help me?’” Schulz said.

Schulz said it is easy to feel powerless when facing serious debt, but resources are available. Creditors can be contacted directly, and nonprofit credit counselors are available for guidance at any time. Schulz said third-party organizations, including local government programs and religious organizations, may also be able to help.

media:content.media:description: Personal bankruptcy filings up nearly 50% since 2022, analysis finds

item.title: High school teacher fired after offering students extra credit in return for cash donations, reports say
item.dc:creator: Akim Powell
item.description: An Iowa high school teacher has been fired for offering students extra credit in return for cash donations to her personal GoFundMe account.
item.content:encoded:
(Gray News) - An Iowa high school teacher has been fired for offering students extra credit in return for cash donations to her personal GoFundMe account.

Stephanie Mullaley, a teacher at a high school in the Clinton Community School District, told students in spring 2026 that she had set up a GoFundMe page to raise money for what she described as “personal education goals,” the Iowa Capital Dispatch reported.

Mullaley allegedly told her students that she had set up a the fundraiser to help pay for her education, adding that if they made cash donations to her account they could earn extra credit toward their grade in her class.

Some students in the class contributed funds to the GoFundMe account, according to Administrative Law Judge Duane Golden. Because of the extra credit incentive, students felt pressured to donate money to the GoFundMe.

Donations, she allegedly wrote would be used to pay for “transportation, including flights, buses, and boats, food and hotel accommodations.”

She was fired on May 29, 2026, for allegedly violating the district’s ethics policy.

Golden denied Mullaley’s request for unemployment benefits, ruling that her conduct amounted to job-related misconduct and demonstrated a “willful or wanton disregard” of her employer’s interests, rendering her ineligible for benefits.

The Iowa Capital Dispatch could not reach Mullaley for comment.

The account had a fundraising goal of $1,800 and netted $140 through six donations ranging from $5 to $50 before activity on the account was paused.

media:content.media:description: An Iowa high school teacher has been fired for offering students extra credit in return for cash donations to her personal GoFundMe account.

item.title: ‘Shouldn’t have taken 31 years’: Victim’s niece voices frustration before Christa Pike’s botched execution
item.dc:creator: Jake Pietrasz, Akim Powell
item.description: Colleen Slemmer’s niece said the process of executing Christa Pike should not have taken 31 years.
item.content:encoded:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) - Colleen Slemmer’s niece said the process of executing Christa Pike should not have taken 31 years.

After learning the state was fighting to lift the stay, Seeley expressed both frustration with the delay and hope that the high court would finally deliver closure.

“It didn’t make sense how they stopped it an hour before she was supposed to go,” Seeley said. “I think that they had enough time out of the 31 years to be able to do this. Colleen is going to get justice today.”

Slemmer was 19 years old when she was killed in January 1995 after being lured to an isolated area on the University of Tennessee agricultural campus. Both Slemmer and Pike were enrolled in Job Corps at the time.

Pike and two co-defendants, Tadaryl Shipp and Shadolla Peterson, were convicted in 1996. Testimony showed the trio tortured Slemmer, carved a pentagram into her chest, and Pike kept a piece of Slemmer’s skull as a souvenir.

Members of Slemmer’s family traveled to the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville on Wednesday morning expecting the execution to take place, but the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals suddenly granted a stay.

Seeley said she spoke with her grandmother, May Martinez, by video call earlier in the day while the family prepared for what they hoped would be the end of a decadeslong legal fight.

Seeley’s mother, who was Slemmer’s sister, passed away in 2021, and Seeley’s stepfather traveled to the prison to stand in her place.

Seeley pushed back against Pike’s repeated legal attempts to overturn her death sentence or obtain clemency.

“It shouldn’t have taken 30, 31 years to be able to get this,” Seeley said. “Allowing somebody, what Christa did to my aunt, to allow her to live 31 years longer than her is heartbreaking.”

Tennessee officials were unable to execute Christa Gail Pike on Wednesday for the 1995 murder after administering two doses of a lethal drug.

Her attorneys filed an emergency motion to halt the execution, saying Pike was “still alive and snoring” after receiving the lethal injection Wednesday.

“The vein in my arm feels like it’s about to bust,” one witness recalled her saying.

According to the emergency motion, the Tennessee Department of Correction began the execution of Pike at about 9 p.m. ET. The motion says that both syringes of pentobarbital were administered and that Pike “has not lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat and is audibly snoring.”

The emergency motion filed Wednesday night stated that the execution was “causing Ms. Pike unnecessary agony and occurring in violation of [her] right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment.”

The motion also demanded the Tennessee Department of Correction immediately begin lifesaving measures.

The 50-year-old inmate was taken by ambulance from the prison, her attorneys said. She was being treated at a hospital.

media:content.media:description: Slemmer was killed in 1995 by Christa Pike and Tadaryl Shipp
